claims.summary: For peripheral parenteral nutrition, ASPEN, in a general PN recommendation, suggests up to 900 mOsm/L and says a safe higher limit is unproven [Boullata2014], NICE declined to set a concentration [NICE2020], ESPEN is reported at 850 mOsm/L and NICUs frequently use 1000 mOsm/L [Fessler2021], and retrospective neonatal data found no more line events above 900 mOsm/L [Cies2014] or at 1000 to 1250 mOsm/L, although the only 2 patients with severity score 4 were at ≥ 1000 mOsm/L [Fessler2021], and no fewer infiltrates after a limit of 1000 was lowered to 900 mOsm/L [Szachnowicz2024]; for other infusions, a neonatal vascular access consensus lists drugs with osmolarity > 600 mOsm/L among non-peripherally compatible solutions, as an example within a UVC indication that cites general infusion standards [Barone2023]; all these values are osmolarity, not osmolality.
claims.note: Current evidence suggests no agreed peripheral limit for parenteral nutrition in neonates: guidance gives 850 to 900 mOsm/L, NICUs often use 1000 mOsm/L, and retrospective neonatal data show no clear rise in line events above 900 or 1000 mOsm/L [Boullata2014; Fessler2021; Cies2014; Szachnowicz2024]. For infusions other than parenteral nutrition, a neonatal consensus gives osmolarity > 600 mOsm/L as an example of a solution not compatible with peripheral access [Barone2023].

evidence.quote: We suggest that PN with an osmolarity up to 900 mOsm/L can be safely infused peripherally. Higher osmolarity limits, especially when peripheral PN is prepared as a TNA, may also be tolerated, but the evidence to support a safe limit is lacking.
evidence.location: Summary table, Question 2, grade Weak (general PN recommendation, not shown as neonate-specific)

evidence.quote: the committee agreed that it was not possible to recommend a specific safe concentration for parenteral nutrition delivered peripherally because of the wide range of concentrations used in the different groups in the study.
evidence.location: Rationale and impact, Venous access (recommendations 1.2.1 and 1.2.2)

evidence.quote: Moreover, the European Society for Parenteral and Enteral Nutrition recommends an even more conservative cutoff (i.e., 850 mOsm/L) for PPN.6
Neonatal intensive care units frequently use higher osmolarity cutoffs (e.g., 1000 mOsm/L) than recommended by ASPEN in order to avoid placing central catheters for short-term PN administration.4,5
There were no significant differences in the incidence of line-related complications in NICU patients receiving PPN with osmolarities 1000 to 1250 versus < 1000 mOsm/L.
However, 2 patients in the ≥ 1000 mOsm/L group had a complication severity score of 4, whereas there were none in the < 1000 mOsm/L group (see Tables 5 and 6).
For neonatal PPNs, the incidence of line-related events was 50 per 100 patient days and 52 per 100 patient days for PPNs ≤ 900 and > 900 mOsm/L (RR = 1.02, 95% CI 0.88-1.18).

A lower PPN osmolarity limit of 900 mOsm/L significantly limited the ability to provide goal amino acid and IVFE doses to NICU patients compared to the previous osmolarity limit of 1000 mOsm/L without reducing the incidence of PIV infiltration or extravasation.

omissions.topic: Humidity and individual tailoring of starting fluids
omissions.note: Current evidence suggests the European guideline attaches its starting volume to a humidified incubator and to tailoring by serum sodium, urine output and weight loss (D1) [Sweet2026].

evidence.quote: Most babies should be started on intravenous fluids of 70–80 mL/kg/day in a humidified incubator although some very immature babies may need more (C1). Fluids must be tailored individually according to serum sodium levels, urine output and weight loss (D1).
evidence.location: Early Fluids and Nutritional Support, Recommendation 2
